![](images/Jupyter.png)

Welcome to your first hands-on session. Over the next hour you'll get comfortable
with the tools you'll use every day in this course, and throughout MEDS: the
**JupyterLab** environment and the **Jupyter Notebooks** you'll write your code in.

::: {.center-text .body-text-m}
Always remember: [**Python is the programming language. JupyterLab is the IDE.**]{.teal-text}
:::

An *IDE* (integrated development environment) is a workspace that puts your code,
its output, your notes, and your files together in one place. JupyterLab is the IDE we
use. Python is the language we write in it.

## Meet JupyterLab

We run JupyterLab on a shared **Posit Workbench** server, so there's nothing to install.
Everything happens in your browser.

#### Step 1: Log in to Posit Workbench

1. Open a browser and go to [workbench-1.bren.ucsb.edu](https://workbench-1.bren.ucsb.edu).
2. Enter your login credentials to access the server.

#### Step 2: Launch a JupyterLab session

1. Click **New Session** and select **JupyterLab** from the list of options.

   ![](images/JupyterLab_launch.png)

2. Click **Start Session** (you don't need to change the Session Name or Cluster). Your
   browser will join the session automatically once the server starts it.

#### Step 3: Get your bearings

When the session launches you'll see the JupyterLab interface. The main pieces are the
**Menu Bar** (top), the **Sidebar / file browser** (left), and the **Main Work Area**
(center), where the Launcher opens first.

![](images/interface-jupyterlab.png)

As you work, JupyterLab adds tabs and panes for notebooks, figures, and terminals. You
can drag them around to arrange your workspace however you like. The
[JupyterLab User Guide](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/index.html) has
much more if you're curious.

::: {.callout-note}
An IDE like JupyterLab supports **interactive computing**: you run your code a piece at a
time and see each result immediately. That fast feedback loop is what makes it great for
exploring data.
:::

## Two ways to run Python

JupyterLab can run your Python code in two places. It's worth seeing both once so you
know the difference.

### The IPython console (a REPL)

From the Launcher, you can open a **Console**, which gives you an *IPython* prompt. This is
a **REPL**, which stands for Read-Eval-Print Loop.

::: {.callout-note}
A **REPL** **R**eads what you type, **E**valuates it, **P**rints the result, and **L**oops
back for more. It's an interactive prompt for trying one line at a time.
:::

Type an expression at the prompt and press Enter, and the REPL evaluates it and shows the
result right away:

```python
21 * 2
```

```
42
```

That's the whole read-eval-print idea: you typed an expression, it evaluated it, it printed
`42`. We're just watching the environment work here. You'll learn Python's syntax properly
this afternoon, and its full set of operators on Day 3. To leave the console REPL, type
`exit()`.

### Jupyter Notebooks (what we'll use)

For the rest of this course you'll write your code in **Jupyter Notebooks**. A notebook lets
you combine **code**, its **output**, and **narrative text** in one document, so your
analysis and the story of your analysis live together. That's exactly what you want for data
science, so notebooks are our home base from here on.

## Getting Started

Let's make the notebook you'll use for this session. **We follow this same setup ritual at
the start of every session**, so it will quickly become second nature.

1. **Create a new notebook:**
   - Click the `+` button in the top left to open a new Launcher.
   - Under **Notebook**, click **eds217_2026** to create a new Python notebook using our
     course environment.

2. **Rename your notebook:**
   - Right-click on the `Untitled.ipynb` tab (see the note below if right-click gives you
     trouble).
   - Select **Rename**.
   - Name it with the format: `Session_1A_JupyterLab.ipynb`

:::{.callout-tip title="Right-clicking in JupyterLab"}
Some browser and operating-system combinations won't hand right-clicks to the JupyterLab
interface and will show a system menu instead. In those cases, `CTRL-Right Click` or
`OPTION-Right Click` usually brings up the Jupyter menu.
:::

3. **Add a title cell:**
   - Click the first cell, and change its type to **Markdown** (dropdown in the toolbar).
   - Add the following content (update the date to today):

```markdown
# Day 1: Session 1A - JupyterLab & Jupyter Notebooks

[Session Webpage](https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/course-materials/interactive-sessions/1a_jupyterlab_notebooks.html)

Date: 08/31/2026
```

4. **Add a code cell** below the title cell (leave it as a **Code** cell). This is where
   you'll start writing Python.

:::{.callout-caution}
Save your work frequently. Click the save icon or press `Ctrl+S` (`Cmd+S` on macOS).
:::

Throughout the session: take notes in Markdown cells, write and run code in Code cells,
and ask questions whenever you need to.

## Working with cells

A notebook is a stack of **cells**. Two kinds matter to us:

- **Code cells** for writing and running Python.
- **Markdown cells** for writing formatted text (notes, headings, links).

### Running a code cell

Click into your empty code cell, type the classic first line of code, and run it with
`Shift + Enter`:

```{python}
print("Hello, Jupyter!")
```

The output appears directly below the cell. `Shift + Enter` runs the cell and moves to the
next one. `Ctrl + Enter` (`Cmd + Enter`) runs it and stays put.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Change the message inside the quotes to greet yourself by name, then re-run the cell with
`Shift + Enter`. Did the output update?
:::

### Writing a Markdown cell

Add a new cell, switch it to **Markdown**, and try some formatting:

```markdown
## My notes

This is a **Markdown** cell. I can write:

- **Bold** with `**text**`
- *Italic* with `*text*`
- [Links](https://jupyterlab.readthedocs.io/)
```

Run the Markdown cell (`Shift + Enter`) to **render** it into formatted text.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
Add one more bullet to your Markdown cell, a link to the course website, then re-render
it. Try double-clicking the rendered cell to edit it again.
:::

### Command mode vs. edit mode

A cell is in one of two modes:

- **Edit mode** (blue bar, cursor in the cell): you're typing *inside* the cell. Press
  `Enter` or click into a cell to enter edit mode.
- **Command mode** (cell selected, no cursor): keystrokes act on the *cell itself*. Press
  `Esc` to enter command mode, then, for example, `b` adds a cell **b**elow, `a` adds one
  **a**bove, and `m` turns the selected cell into **M**arkdown.

## Handy JupyterLab features

A few features that will save you time all week:

- **Tab completion:** start typing a name and press `Tab` to auto-complete it or see
  suggestions.
- **Built-in help:** type `help(print)` in a code cell to read a function's documentation,
  or add a `?` after a name (`print?`) for a quick description.
- **The Variable Inspector:** shows the names, types, and values of everything you've
  defined. Open it from the Command Palette (`View > Activate Command Palette`, then type
  "variable inspector") or with `Ctrl + Shift + I` (`Cmd + Shift + I` on Mac).
- **Magic commands:** IPython adds special commands prefixed with `%`, like `%history` to
  see what you've run. You'll meet these as needed.

:::{.callout-tip title="✏️ Test your knowledge"}
In a code cell, type `pri` and press `Tab`. Does JupyterLab offer to complete it to
`print`? Then run `help(print)` and skim the description.
:::

## Saving and exporting

- **Save:** the save icon, or `Ctrl + S` / `Cmd + S`. Do this often.
- **Export:** JupyterLab can export a notebook to other formats (HTML, PDF, and more) via
  `File > Export Notebook As`. This is handy for sharing a finished analysis.

## Key Points

- **Python is the language. JupyterLab is the IDE** you run it in, hosted on Posit
  Workbench, so it's all in your browser.
- JupyterLab can run Python in a **REPL** (a read-eval-print console) or in **notebooks**,
  and we use notebooks from here on.
- A notebook combines **code cells**, their **output**, and **Markdown** narrative in one
  document.
- Run a cell with `Shift + Enter`. Use `Esc` and `Enter` to switch between **command** and
  **edit** mode.
- Start every session with the same ritual: **create, rename, title cell, save often.**
